title: Hydration Strategies
description: Master hydration techniques to coordinate server-side and client-side data in React Query.

data.text: Welcome to this comprehensive guide on **Hydration Strategies**. Master hydration techniques to coordinate server-side and client-side data in React Query. In today's rapidly evolving technology landscape, understanding this topic is crucial for any developer looking to build robust, scalable, and maintainable applications. This lesson will take you from fundamental concepts to advanced implementations, providing you with practical knowledge you can apply immediately. Whether you are a beginner taking your first steps or an experienced developer looking to deepen your expertise, this guide has something valuable for you. We will explore theoretical foundations, practical implementations, real-world scenarios, and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end of this lesson, you will have a thorough understanding of Hydration Strategies and be confident in applying it to your projects.
What is Hydration?

In React Query, hydration means calling `hydrate` with the serialized cache state from the server. This merges the server data into the client QueryClient before any components render. As a result, `useQuery` immediately returns the server data instead of showing a loading state.
Avoiding Hydration Mismatches

A hydration mismatch happens when the server-rendered HTML does not match the client's initial render. React Query's hydration system prevents this by ensuring cached data is available synchronously. However, you must still follow strict rules to avoid subtle bugs.

data.title: Correct Hydration Pattern
Consistent Query Keys
data.text: Use identical query keys on the server and client. A mismatch between `['user', id]` on the server and `['user', String(id)]` on the client creates a cache miss and forces a refetch.
Parallel Data Fetching

Server-side, you can prefetch multiple queries in parallel using `Promise.all`. This is critical for avoiding waterfalls where each query waits for the previous one to finish. Parallel fetching reduces total server response time and improves Time to First Byte (TTFB).

data.text: Cache Time Considerations

Server-fetched data should generally have a longer `staleTime` because it was just fetched. Setting `staleTime` to a few minutes ensures the client does not immediately refetch fresh data. However, `gcTime` controls how long inactive data stays in memory, so balance these based on your app's memory constraints.

data.title: Memory Leaks
data.text: Setting `gcTime` to Infinity keeps data forever, which can cause memory leaks in long-running apps. Use a reasonable value like 5 minutes unless you have a specific reason to extend it.
Partial Hydration

You do not need to hydrate every query. If a query is only used client-side or depends on user interaction, skip it during SSR. Partial hydration reduces serialized payload size and keeps your initial HTML focused on above-the-fold content.

Key Takeaways
points: Hydration transfers server cache to the client
Use identical query keys to prevent cache misses
Match staleTime to data freshness needs
Guard against memory leaks with reasonable gcTime
data.takeaway: Proper hydration ensures zero duplicate requests and instant client-side rendering.

data.text: Common Mistakes to Avoid

Even experienced developers can fall into these traps when working with **Hydration Strategies**. Being aware of these common mistakes will help you write better code and avoid costly debugging sessions:

items: **Over-Engineering**: Using advanced features of Hydration Strategies when a simple solution suffices. Always start with the simplest approach that meets your requirements and add complexity only when justified.
**Ignoring Edge Cases**: Failing to handle null values, empty states, and boundary conditions leads to runtime errors and poor user experience.
**Copy-Paste Without Understanding**: Using code snippets without fully understanding their implications creates hidden bugs and security vulnerabilities.
**Neglecting Testing**: Assuming code works without tests is a recipe for production incidents. Write tests that verify behavior and prevent regressions.
**Performance Blindness**: Ignoring performance implications until they become critical issues. Profile early and optimize based on data, not assumptions.
**Hardcoding Configuration**: Embedding values directly in code instead of using environment variables and configuration files.
**Tight Coupling**: Creating dependencies that make code difficult to test, modify, or reuse. Favor composition over inheritance.
**Inconsistent Error Handling**: Mixing different error handling patterns makes code unpredictable and hard to debug.

data.text: Performance Considerations

Performance is a critical aspect of any production application. When implementing **Hydration Strategies**, consider these optimization strategies to ensure your application remains fast and responsive:

items: **Lazy Loading**: Defer non-critical operations until they are actually needed to reduce initial load time.
**Caching**: Implement intelligent caching strategies to avoid redundant computations and network requests.
**Memoization**: Cache results of expensive function calls to improve performance for repeated operations.
**Batch Processing**: Group multiple operations together to reduce overhead and improve throughput.
**Resource Management**: Properly clean up resources, event listeners, and subscriptions to prevent memory leaks.
**Profiling**: Use performance profiling tools to identify bottlenecks before optimizing.
**Bundle Size**: Minimize dependencies and use tree-shaking to reduce application bundle size.
**Network Optimization**: Reduce payload sizes, use compression, and implement efficient data fetching strategies.

data.text: Security Considerations
Security should never be an afterthought. When implementing **Hydration Strategies**, keep these security best practices in mind to protect your application and users:

items: **Input Validation**: Always validate and sanitize user input to prevent injection attacks.
**Authentication and Authorization**: Implement proper access controls and verify user permissions.
**Secrets Management**: Never hardcode API keys, passwords, or tokens. Use environment variables and secret management services.
**HTTPS**: Always use HTTPS in production to encrypt data in transit.
**Content Security Policy**: Implement CSP headers to mitigate XSS attacks.
**Dependency Scanning**: Regularly scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
**Rate Limiting**: Protect APIs from abuse with appropriate rate limiting.
**Audit Logging**: Log security-relevant events for monitoring and incident response.
